newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF starts talks with Bulgaria on new funding.
newsitem.headline: IMF starts talks with Bulgaria on new funding.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) negotiators have started talks with Bulgaria's interim government, warning tough problems must be solved before they can reach a funding agreement to help stabilise the collapsing economy.

"We want to agree as much as possible on the policies needed to stabilise the situation and the work programme to prepare for the currency board," IMF mission leader Anne McGuirk told reporters on Tuesday.

Speaking after meeting interim Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski, she said the Fund saw no obstacles in working with a caretaker cabinet to prepare a new stand-by arrangement involving implementation of a fixed exchange rate system that would stabilise the devastated economy.
McGuirk arrived late on Monday from Brussels where the European Union discussed mobilising help for the crisis-torn country, but the EU decided to act after an agreement with the IMF was in place.

The 15-nation EU said in a statement on Tuesday it was prepared "to take initiatives in order to mobilise support...in parallel with the IMF negotiations and provided a credible economic stabilisation and reform programme is put in place."
Bulgaria relies solely on foreign loans to repay $1 billion of foreign debts due this year alone.
The caretaker cabinet appointed three weeks ago, pledged to speed up sell-offs aiming to boost foreign investment, shut down loss-making state companies and liberalise trade rules.
McGuirk said the Fund was impressed by the interim government's commitment to leading Bulgaria out of the grave crisis and speeding up market reforms delayed in the past seven years.

On Monday, ahead of talks with the IMF, the caretaker cabinet partly lifted controls on bread and grain prices which gave rise to shortages. To counteract them the cabinet unlocked 50,000 tonnes of grain from state reserves.
The cabinet is also expected this week to lift price controls on medicines and cigarettes.

Leaders of major trade unions on Tuesday pledged not to oppose inevitable liberalisation of prices in an agreement signed jointly with Sofianski. The agreement bound monthly wages to companies' financial results and bound the cabinet to pay inflation adjusted compensations to the poor.
"I think there is broad agreement that we will try to work on a new programme with Bulgaria," said McGuirk.
Continuous mishandling of the economy by the previous Socialist government has thrown Bulgaria into chaos, while 30 days of widespread strikes and political squabbling further paralysed it.
In the beginning of February President Petar Stoyanov mediated an agreement to hold an early general election on April 19, dissolved parliament and named a caretaker cabinet headed by Sofianski.

"I believe we will reach a mutually acceptable long-term programme which, with the support of all political forces, will enable us to reach a new stand-by agreement," said Sofianski, whose powers were expanded by the outgoing parliament.

The team is expected to review Bulgaria's slumping economic performance and set arrangements for a currency board system, proposed last year to halt the slump of the national currency, the lev and restore confidence in its crumbling financial system.
The system requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing financial powers of the government and the central bank, thus preventing printing of money.

Asked whether the IMF would provide any funding to meet urgent balance of payment problems before the introduction of the currency board, McGuirk said: "We have a lot of technical work to do before any decisions can be made."

Passing a realistic austerity budget for this year will be one of the first tasks of the new parliament, once elected. Bulgaria's deepening crisis has made obsolete the 1997 budget assumptions drafted by the former Socialist government.

The currency has fallen by some 300 percent against the dollar since the beginning of the year and economists see February inflation at around 100 percent. Monthly inflation last month was 44 percent.
The IMF and the government will also need to seek means to resolve Bulgaria's 1.7 trillion lev ($862.9 million) domestic debt, seen as a hindrance to successful implementation of the currency board.
Central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov saw June as the earliest date for the system's introduction.
($ = 1970 Bulgarian Levs)
